Wednesday, 18 October, after the orchestra rehearsal at the school in La Duchère. Yanis’s mother, Madame Mansouri, has come to talk to Julien. She doesn’t look pleased.
Monsieur Moreau, I’ll be frank. Since he started the cello, Yanis talks about nothing else. The more he plays, the less homework he does.
I understand your concern. But you know, what we generally see is the opposite: the more music children do, the more focused they are at school.
Maybe. But he’s coming home later and later. Last Wednesday he stayed an extra hour to practise.
That’s true, it’s my fault. He absolutely wanted to master a difficult passage. I didn’t dare stop him, all the more so because he wasn’t getting discouraged.
Yanis? Not getting discouraged? At home he gives up on everything after five minutes.
Not here. He’s the pupil who works hardest. He’s progressing faster than the others, and he helps the little ones. His teacher told me he participates more in class.
(silence) His teacher told you that? She never says anything positive to me.
Ask her. And come and listen to a rehearsal, so that you can judge for yourself. Next Wednesday he has a little solo.
A solo? My Yanis? (smiles for the first time) His father will never believe me.
Bring him too. The more parents there are, the more confidence the children will have in themselves.
He works nights, he sleeps in the afternoon… But for a solo he’ll wake up. He was a musician, you know, in Morocco. He played the oud.
The oud? Then maybe that’s where Yanis gets his ear from. He absolutely must come.
All right. I’ll come, and I’ll bring him. But homework first, Monsieur Moreau. As much music as you like, but not less maths.
It’s a deal. I’ll make him do his homework before every rehearsal. You have my word.

At the start of a sentence, "plus" is read "plews" (with s) when followed by a vowel: "plus il joue" = "plew-zeel".
"Doh-tahn": "au" = o, the final t is silent.
"Ood": the final d is heard (Arabic word).
For "the more… the more", French puts PLUS / MOINS at the start of each half of the sentence. No article, no "que", no "autant":
Plus il joue, plus il progresse.
The more he plays, the more he improves.
Plus il joue, moins il fait ses devoirs.
The more he plays, the less homework he does.
Moins on dort, moins on est concentré.
Plus il y aura de parents, plus les enfants auront confiance.
The more parents there are, the more confident the children will be.
Common mistakes: "Le plus il joue, le plus…" (no article) and "Plus il joue, et plus…" (possible in speech, but not needed). With nouns: "plus DE musique, plus DE confiance".

Il rentre de plus en plus tard.

"D’autant plus que" (all the more so because) adds a cause that REINFORCES something already said. "D’autant moins que" does the opposite:
I didn’t dare stop him, all the more so because he wasn’t getting discouraged.
I understand it all the less because yesterday he was happy.
Il lit autant que sa sœur.
Autant de musique que de mathématiques.
C’est l’élève qui travaille le plus.
"Davantage" is not used before an adjective: "plus grand", not "davantage grand". It goes after the verb or at the end: "Il faut travailler davantage."
Je lui ferai faire ses devoirs.
Venez, pour que vous jugiez par vous-même.

After the inauguration, rehearsals began in earnest. Every Wednesday afternoon, Julien took the bus to La Duchère, with a suitcase full of scores and a bag of spare strings. The more the weeks went by, the heavier the suitcase became, and the later Julien came home.

The school’s covered playground wasn’t made for music. The sound bounced off the walls, the chairs squeaked, and at half past four the older kids’ basketball banged regularly against the door. But the children didn’t care. For them, it was the most beautiful concert hall in the world.

At first there were thirty of them. By October there were thirty-six. Brothers and sisters turned up, cousins, neighbours. Julien didn’t have enough instruments for everyone. He had the newcomers share a violin in pairs, taking turns, which led to endless arguments.

Radu and Lucia came to help as soon as they had a free moment between classes on their master’s course. Lucia took care of the guitars, Radu of the rhythm. He had invented a system: the children who had no instrument banged on plastic buckets. The harder they banged, the happier they were.

Yanis progressed faster than all the others. He arrived first and left last. He had learned to hold the bow, to tune his cello, to read the notes. Julien had never seen a child learn so fast, all the more so because Yanis had never touched an instrument before September.

On Wednesday 25 October, as promised, Madame Mansouri came to listen to the rehearsal. She sat at the back, very upright, her bag on her knees. Beside her was a tall, tired man, with the red eyes of someone who works nights. It was Yanis’s father. He said nothing.

When Yanis saw his parents, he went bright red. During the first piece he missed several notes. Julien could see his hands shaking. The harder he tried to do well, the less he managed. So Julien stopped the orchestra and went over to him.

"Close your eyes," he told him softly. "Forget they’re here. Play as if you were alone in your room." Yanis closed his eyes. He took a deep breath. And when the orchestra started again, he played his little solo, eight very simple bars, with a full, warm sound that filled the whole hall.

When he opened his eyes, his father was standing. He wasn’t crying, he wasn’t smiling. He was looking at his son as if he were seeing him for the first time. Then he went over to Julien and shook his hand for a very long time, without a word, with a strength that said everything.

The following week, Monsieur Mansouri came back. This time he was carrying a strange case, shaped like a pear. He opened it in front of the children: it was an oud, with a round belly of pale wood and a short neck. "My father gave it to me when I was Yanis’s age," he said. "I haven’t played since I came to France."

He tuned the instrument slowly, frowning. Then he played. A melody from his village, somewhere between Fès and the mountains. The children fell silent, even the chattiest ones. Lucia picked up her guitar and searched for the chords. Radu tapped the rhythm softly on a bucket.

And Yanis, without anyone asking him, picked up his cello and played a long, low note under his father’s melody. Then another. Then another again. They played together, father and son, for five minutes. It was the first time in their lives.

That same evening, Julien told Ioana about it while giving Rose-Hélène her bottle. She was eight months old now. She could sit up on her own, she grabbed everything within reach, and she had a passion for the piano: as soon as you sat her in front of the keyboard, she banged on it, laughing.

"The harder she bangs, the more she laughs," Ioana remarked. "Like Radu’s kids with the buckets." Julien laughed. "She’ll be a percussionist. Or an architect, like her mother, and she’ll build concert halls for her father." Rose-Hélène banged even harder, as if giving her opinion.

On 8 November, the mayor called Julien. He had spoken to the region, as promised. The budget vote would take place on Thursday 14 December. "I’ll be frank," he said. "It’s not in the bag. Many councillors think music is a luxury. The more we can show that people support the project, the better our chances."

That same evening, Ioana had an idea: a petition. She drafted it in an hour, with the help of Nathalie, who was used to administrative paperwork. The text was short and clear: "So that music is a right for all children, and not a privilege, we support the Musique en partage project."

Signatures came in from everywhere, faster and faster. The Fourvière residents signed first, led by Madame Lambert, who had corrected two mistakes in the text. Then the parents of La Duchère, the shopkeepers of the Croix-Rousse, Julien’s colleagues, Sophie’s customers, who had put a sheet next to the till.

Monsieur Garnier put the petition in his shop window, next to a violin. Odile sent it to all her former colleagues at the hospital. Karim shared it with his students. Even the driver of the care home minibus got everyone who boarded to sign it.

After a week, there were a thousand signatures. After two weeks, three thousand. The local papers began to talk about it. An article appeared with a photo of Yanis and his father, the cello and the oud side by side. The headline read: "More than an orchestra, a family."

Madame Mansouri cut out the article and stuck it on the fridge door. She told Julien she had also sent it to her mother in Morocco, and to all her aunts. "Now the whole village knows my son plays the cello," she said proudly. "And his maths marks have gone up. I check."

Even Hélène threw herself into the campaign. Every afternoon she set herself up in the care home’s entrance hall with the petition and a pen, and she accepted no excuses. The visitors who came to see their parents all left with one signature fewer and one smile more. "The older I get," she would say, "the more stubborn I am."

At the end of November, an official letter arrived at the Conservatoire. Claire Vasseur opened it in front of Julien, her hands trembling a little. The regional council was inviting the La Duchère orchestra to play in front of the councillors on 14 December, just before the vote. Ten minutes, no more.

"Ten minutes," Claire repeated. "To convince a hundred and fifty councillors that music isn’t a luxury." Julien smiled. "With Yanis, Inès and thirty-six children banging on buckets, I think we can do it." Claire laughed for the first time in weeks.

That evening, Julien told the children the news. There were shouts of joy, then an anxious silence. A little girl raised her hand. "Sir, what’s a councillor?" Julien thought. "It’s someone who makes decisions for a lot of people. And on 14 December, you’re the ones who are going to help them decide."

Yanis raised his hand in turn. "And what if we play out of tune?" Julien looked at Inès, who was clutching Lucien’s clarinet. Then he gave the answer Madame Roux had taught him: "Then play out of tune, but play with your heart. The more you play with your heart, the less they’ll notice the wrong notes."

That evening, on his way home, Julien walked past Sophie’s bakery. On the sheet next to the till there were three pages of signatures. Right at the bottom, in a clumsy childish hand, someone had signed: "Rose-Hélène, 8 months". Right next to it, Ioana had drawn a little heart.

Julien took the pen tied to the sheet with a piece of string, and he signed too, just below his daughter. Then, after hesitating for a moment, he added one last name, in very straight letters: "Henri Bernard, sailor". Sophie, behind her counter, pretended not to see anything. But she smiled.

Inès, the girl with the clarinet, keeps a diary. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Wednesday. Today I went to see Madame Roux at the care home, like every Wednesday. The more I see her, the more I love her. She teaches me things about Lucien, her husband.
He played the clarinet in a brass band. He played out of tune, but he played loudly. Madame Roux says the louder he played, the more people danced. I play better and better, but not very loudly yet.
At first I was afraid of playing wrong notes. Now I play fewer and fewer. Monsieur Moreau says it doesn’t matter, all the more so because Lucien played lots of them.
My mother thinks I practise my instrument as much as I do my homework. It’s not true: I practise the clarinet more. But my marks at school are better than before, so she doesn’t say anything.

Madame Roux asked me whether I’d like to play at the December concert, in front of the regional council. I said yes. The more I think about it, the more stage fright I get. But she’ll be in the front row.
Before I left, she told me: "Play with your heart, like Lucien." I promised her. This evening I’m going to practise for another hour, so that I’m ready. But maths first.
